what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-1 to recommend disapproval of Article 4, a transfer from free cash to the special education reserve fund.
The board deferred Articles 2 and 3, and separately Article 9 (track and field engineering), to be voted on after the town knows its certified free cash.
The board recommended approval of Articles 1, 5 and 6, took no position 4-1 on the non-binding straw polls in Articles 7 and 8, and approved the warrant.
A motion to have the town manager draft a special education reserve fund policy was withdrawn; the matter goes to the school committee chair for their agenda first.
The town manager reported that year-end close is slow and free cash may not be certified in time for the special town meeting.

why_it_matters: Several warrant articles depend on free cash, and until it is certified the board cannot finalize recommendations on them, so voters at the special town meeting may be asked to act on items the board has not yet weighed in on.

Article 4 would move money from free cash into a special education reserve, a fund that cushions the town budget, which is mostly taxes, against unplanned placement costs, and the board's recommendation against it is advisory only; Town Meeting makes the decision.
watch_next: Nov 17: the board meets at 6:30, before the special town meeting, to vote on the deferred articles, then Town Meeting votes on the warrant.
Nov 10: Select Board meeting, partly a workshop on the draft flag policy.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to place the middle high school track and field engineering article on the special town meeting warrant.
The board voted 0-5 on the accessibility and park design article, which was moved so it could be voted down, and it did not go on the warrant.
The advisory article on stormwater funding mechanisms passed 4-1, and the trust fund continuity article failed 0-5.
The board approved the Kiku liquor license unanimously with the annual fee cut to one quarter for the rest of the calendar year.
In a joint session, the Stormwater Task Force and the board discussed a utility fee versus the operating budget; the track article was later moved to last on the warrant.

why_it_matters: Voters at the special town meeting will be asked to act on design and engineering for the track and field retaining wall, which could lead to a later construction request and tax impact.
The stormwater advisory article asks voters to weigh a dedicated utility fee against paying through the operating budget, which is funded mostly by taxes.
watch_next: October 27 Select Board meeting, where the board will make its recommendations on all special town meeting warrant articles.
The November 3 election, whose warrant the board approved, and the special town meeting warrant as finalized.

meetings.headline: Select Board advanced the Food Pantry's temporary move to 30 School Street, waiving fees and OK'ing a license.
meetings.summary: The board presented three staff Merit Awards, publicly introduced new town manager Jessica "Jack" Miller, and voted to authorize a license agreement and waive building fees advancing the Lunenburg Food Pantry's temporary relocation to 30 School Street, amid public-comment dispute over whether that structure is "permanent" or "temporary." The board also referred zoning cleanup and stormwater-fee articles to the planning board for the November special town meeting, accepted a donated boulder for town hall, discussed but declined for now a MassWorks grant to study senior housing at the former TCP school, and debated (and largely declined) moving to a biweekly meeting schedule.

budget_items.what_was_said: The food pantry president said an amateur online estimate of applicable fees came to around this figure; the town manager listed building, wiring, plumbing, gas, sheet metal and technology fees as ones the select board could waive.
The town manager gave an off-the-cuff guess for the cost of a full reclamation of the potholed parking lot near the food pantry site, while the town looks into interim patching before winter.
Town and school staff are still reconciling FY26 close-out, including where the operating budget intersects with special revenue and grant funds, expected to finish in roughly two to three weeks.
Colonial Power was selected for a fixed-term supply contract; residents will get postcards about the new rate with a 30-day window to opt out before the November switchover.

A proposed special town meeting article would replace fixed dollar fee figures in the stormwater bylaw with a reference to the planning board's fee schedule as amended from time to time; referred to the planning board.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager proposed using the town's opioid settlement fund to replace AEDs, each costing roughly this amount with about a ten-year lifespan, across town and school buildings and police/fire vehicles.

budget_items.what_was_said: A board member cited a reported cost range to prepare a grant proposal exploring senior housing at the former TCP school, and argued the town could not fund that effort now.

budget_items.what_was_said: A resident, citing the state's end-of-year report, said athletics spending and the share covered by user fees changed sharply between fiscal 2017 and fiscal 2025.
The same resident said the dollar amount of athletics costs carried by taxpayers rather than fees rose over eight years.
The resident said general-fund transportation spending rose over four years as part of a broader cost trend he wanted the board to weigh.

budget_items.topic: Median household income of families with children in the schools
budget_items.what_was_said: The resident cited census data putting this group's median household income as the highest of any in town, as context for who bears extracurricular costs.

budget_items.topic: Tax-base share of extracurricular program costs
budget_items.what_was_said: The resident said most of the cost of extracurricular programs is carried by the broader tax base rather than by user fees.

budget_items.topic: Diesel fuel cost and school transportation budget
budget_items.what_was_said: A board member warned diesel prices approaching this figure could push transportation costs up again heading into next budget season.
A board member said a preliminary report indicated health insurance premiums could rise by about this percentage, cautioning the next budget season will likely be harder than last.

decisions.decision: The Brooks House long-term sale/lease report will be presented by subject-matter experts (planning, economic development and facilities staff) at the November special town meeting, closing out the November 2024 non-binding vote directive.

The boards/committees/commissions handbook review will be broken into roughly four rounds, with the first six chapters to be discussed at a future meeting in about two weeks; the remote-participation chapter will be handled separately.
The board will not pursue a MassWorks grant to study senior housing at the former TCP school this grant cycle, saying more public discussion is needed first.

Rather than adopt a strict every-other-week meeting schedule, the board will keep its default weekly Tuesday slot and cancel individual meetings as needed, with time-critical votes handled remotely if necessary.
The town manager will get PACC vendor quotes for audio/camera upgrades to the middle high school collaborative room, to evaluate it as an additional accessible meeting location.

meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board held a public hearing under MGL c.140 §157 on a nuisance-dog complaint filed by George and Jennifer Burden against neighbors Charles and Stacy Cordmash. The complainant declined to testify, while the investigating detective, the animal control officer, the dog owner, and a neighboring HOA trustee all testified that they found no evidence of excessive barking or other nuisance behavior; after deliberation the board voted unanimously that the dog is not a nuisance dog, and town counsel was asked to draft the written decision and to consider changing the hearing process going forward.

meetings.summary: A joint Select Board / Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee meeting opened with a presentation on Mass Save energy-summit incentives for building electrification, then shifted to a long workshop on the deteriorating TC Pacios (TCP) building — its failing systems, a history of a double-appropriated roof-repair fund later corrected at town meeting, and whether to repair or demolish it. No formal vote was taken on TCP or the Brooks House, but the group leaned toward not investing further in TCP, tasked the Facilities Director with cost estimates, and agreed the committee will bring formal recommendations on both buildings to a future meeting, with its next meeting set for August 3rd.

meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified a police detective promotion and several routine appointments, heard a lengthy planning-director update and a historical society pitch for a Revolutionary War memorial, and got tangled in a dispute over a stalled Trust Fund Commission appointment. meetings.headline: Amanda Moore resigns as vice chair citing health; board reorganizes and plans a special election
meetings.summary: The Select Board acknowledged the resignations of the vice chair (citing health, amid the aftermath of the failed override) and two town staff members, then reorganized its own leadership, electing a new chair, vice chair and clerk. It also voted on an ambulance-billing write-off, a nuisance dog investigation, waivers for a town event and a right of first refusal, discussed possibly calling a special town meeting on the budget while deferring to the School and Finance Committees, and heard a town manager's report on bridge and flooring project bids and a culvert grant.

A resident said the water district will hold a special meeting on a proposed water treatment plant that would affect water fees charged to all public buildings, including schools.
The purchase price category was excluded from the RFP evaluation criteria given a recent assessment showing the property's value as negative.

meetings.headline: Select Board held final public comment on the override before Saturday's town election; the chair backed a yes vote.
meetings.summary: The Select Board held its final public comment session before Saturday's annual town election and Proposition 2½ override vote, hearing residents both for and against the override, then the chair publicly stated support for the override. The board also ratified a police executive assistant hire, approved two youth achievement proclamations, assigned a police officer (not the elected constable) to cover the election, approved an FY27 state advocacy letter on school funding, voted to sell two tax-title Hollis Road parcels, and entered executive session at the close.

budget_items.what_was_said: A resident argued the town's roughly $1.4 million in new growth revenue was split unevenly, with capital projects, a finance committee reserve above policy, and a new town manager hire funded while schools were left short of level-service funding.
A resident said the added annual tax bill under the override was unreasonable given current gas prices, citing figures for homes in a stated value range.
The board was asked to approve appointing Kimberly Murphy at a specific wage step in addition to ratifying her hire.
The board's advocacy letter urges the senator to increase circuit breaker funding to a stated reimbursement percentage under a specific line item.

budget_items.topic: Section 3 local aid for minimum aid districts
budget_items.what_was_said: The letter urges a minimum per-pupil local aid distribution for minimum aid districts like Lunenburg.
The letter thanks the senator for a proposed increase to statewide UGGA funding, citing the increase and resulting total.

budget_items.topic: Sale of tax-title property, 250 and 356 Hollis Road

minutes.summary: The Select Board finalized its annual town meeting warrant, voting to recommend approval of the FY27 balanced budget, both tiers of the proposed override, and several enterprise fund articles, after lengthy public comment and board debate over cuts to services versus a new assistant town manager position and fourth fire shift. what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to recommend the FY27 balanced budget for town meeting.
The board recommended the override's second tier by a 3-1 vote; the first tier's vote outcome was not audible on the recording.
Public commenters objected to proposed cuts to the library, senior center and beach program alongside new spending on an assistant town manager and a fourth fire shift.
The board also recommended the PAC/PEG, solid waste, water and sewer enterprise fund articles, all unanimously.
The board scheduled a budget public information meeting for the evening of April 28 at the Adult Activity Center.

why_it_matters: Both the balanced budget and the override now go to town meeting, where the choice is between a level-services budget with cuts to programs like the library, senior center and beach program, or an override that funds the assistant town manager position and a fourth fire shift.
A resident weighing the override should note the split board vote on its second tier, which signals the choice was not unanimous even among the officials recommending it.
The April 28 public information meeting is the town's forum for residents to ask about the budget and override before voting.

meetings.headline: Board set the FY27 town meeting warrant and voted a two-tier override question onto the town election ballot
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through the annual town meeting warrant article by article with town counsel, deferring several items (prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, the snow-and-ice closeout, and union contract funding) to town meeting itself, and declining -- after individual members stated concerns -- to include a Trust Fund Commission legal-fees article or a quorum bylaw article that counsel flagged as legally uncertain. The board voted to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, rounding the tiers to clean dollar figures and choosing a "Question 1/Question 2" ballot format, while one member stated ongoing concerns about the override's affordability. It also discussed but did not finalize where the override and other articles should sit in the warrant order and consent agenda.

public_comment.topic: Asked the board to randomize/lottery the order of non-fixed warrant articles at town meeting to stop "vote stacking" around the override.

Clarified the "rule of necessity" legal doctrine behind the trust fund quorum article and said the commission has filed a breach-of-fiduciary-duty notice against the town with a 30-day response request.

what_happened.line: Board voted 5-0 to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, pending town counsel's final edits.
Board members individually declined to put two Trust Fund Commission articles, on legal fees and a quorum bylaw, on the town meeting warrant.
The board deferred several FY27 warrant items, including prior-year invoices and union contract funding, to town meeting itself.
A Trust Fund Commission representative told the board the commission has filed a notice of breach of fiduciary duty against the town.

why_it_matters: The override question, if it proceeds as set, will ask voters at the annual town election to approve additional property tax collection above the state cap, split into two tiers residents can vote on separately.

Sending prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, and union contract funding to town meeting itself means those costs will be settled by the voters present rather than decided in advance by the board.
The declined Trust Fund Commission articles and the fiduciary-duty notice point to an unresolved dispute between that commission and the town that may surface again at town meeting.
watch_next: FY27 annual town meeting vote on the deferred warrant articles and the override question

meetings.headline: Board included nearly all FY27 warrant articles; TC Passios' safety issues leave the food pantry's future unresolved.
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through most of the draft FY2027 annual town meeting warrant, voting to include (and in some cases recommend) dozens of articles covering capital cleanup items, union contract funding, an OPEB trust appropriation, a vacation-buyout liability reduction, and several bylaw changes, while holding off on the override placeholder, trust fund commission articles, a stormwater bylaw, and the Central Mass Mosquito Control article pending more information. The board also heard an extended, unresolved presentation from the Lunenburg Community Food Pantry about the deteriorating TC Passios building, where the food pantry currently operates, and closed a public hearing on opting out of mail-in early voting before entering executive session to discuss a collective bargaining agreement.

what_happened.line: The board voted to include most of the draft FY2027 town meeting warrant, including the Prop 2.5 override placeholder article, without recommending it.
It held off on the trust fund commission bylaw and legal-fees articles, a stormwater utility bylaw, and Central Mass Mosquito Control participation, pending legal review or more resident input.
An extended presentation on the deteriorating TC Passios building, where the food pantry operates, ended without a decision on relocation or the building's future.
The board closed a public hearing and voted unanimously to opt out of mail-in early voting for local elections this year.
The board entered executive session to discuss a collective bargaining agreement; that portion of the recording has no audio.

why_it_matters: Residents will see a Prop 2.5 override placeholder on the FY2027 warrant, though the board has not recommended it, so it will be a question voters take up at town meeting.
The food pantry's future home is unresolved: the board said it will not fund TC Passios roof or heating repairs without a broader plan for the building.
A handful of warrant articles -- a stormwater bylaw, mosquito control participation, and trust fund commission bylaws -- are still open and could return changed before town meeting.

meetings.headline: Select Board leaned toward a two-tier (core + restoration) joint town/school override, no vote taken
meetings.summary: The Select Board spent a line-by-line workshop walking through every department's FY27 budget changes since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging cuts (police clerk, second SRO, fire per diem, recreation director, communications/IT, animal control, town clerk staffing) as candidates to restore if an override passes. By the end the board leaned toward a tiered override structure (a core/level-service budget plus a separate restoration ask, for both town and school) but took no formal vote on it, and set a deadline of Thursday for the town's restoration number and Wednesday for the school committee's numbers.

what_happened.line: The Select Board leaned toward a two-tier override structure -- a core budget plus a separate restoration ask -- for both town and school, without taking a formal vote.

Board members worked line by line through department cuts made since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging items such as a police clerk position, a second school resource officer, fire department per diem coverage, the recreation director post, communications/IT staffing and animal control funding as candidates to restore if an override passes.

The town manager was asked to produce the town's restoration budget number by Thursday, and Thursday's planned Tri-Board meeting was flagged for cancellation or reconsideration so the school committee's core and restoration figures could come in by Wednesday instead.

The board also settled smaller line items along the way, including pursuing a town engineer position in the restoration budget regardless of storm water compliance funding and leaving the snow and ice budget unchanged rather than risk a later cut.

why_it_matters: This is the shape of the override question residents may eventually vote on -- a base town/school budget plus a separate restoration ask, rather than one combined number.
The restoration list touches police staffing, a school resource officer, fire coverage, recreation programming and animal control -- services that stay cut if no override passes.

meetings.headline: Select Board leans toward letting town meeting voters decide on continued mosquito-control funding.
meetings.summary: The select board approved a one-day liquor license, then held a joint meeting with the board of health for an extensive educational presentation by Central Mass Mosquito Control Project on its surveillance, ditch-maintenance, larval and adult mosquito control work, amid a town budget shortfall that has put the district's assessment on the table. No vote was taken on the mosquito control funding; the chair said it should go to town meeting voters. The board also acknowledged a Conservation Commission resignation, heard a brief town manager report on a building leak, and reviewed (without voting on) draft warrant articles for the 2026 annual town meeting before recessing into a tri-board meeting.

why_it_matters: If mosquito control funding goes to town meeting, residents will be asked to vote directly on whether to keep paying into that regional assessment, which a board member said the state sets using a land-mass and valuation formula rather than local choice.

The draft warrant articles reviewed -- a new revolving fund, a capital reallocation, and a policy change to vacation buyouts -- are early-stage and not yet committed to the warrant, but they preview what voters may see at the 2026 annual town meeting.
A public commenter raised a concern about pesticide safety to bees, which residents may want addressed before any funding vote.

The board dropped a bundled intercom/radio security request and the Fitzgerald field project after learning state guidance caps towns at one to three earmark requests.

why_it_matters: An earmark is a request for state funding outside the town's own budget, so dropping the school intercom and middle-high radio security upgrades from this list means that project now has to compete for town capital dollars instead.
The ranked order signals which project the delegation will push hardest for as the state budget moves through the legislature this session.
This affects the public safety building, the fire department, and the primary school -- not this year's town tax bill, since these are requests to the state, not town appropriations.

what_happened.line: The town manager told the Select Board the preliminary FY27 budget will not balance and will need an override, with the gap as heard put at more than an amount as heard pending final school figures.
Preliminary FY25 free cash is coming in well above what was budgeted, partly from a school turnback, but the capital plan still holds its lower, more conservative figure until numbers are certified.
The board spent most of the meeting revising its FY26 goals line by line and reviewing warrant articles for the 2026 annual town meeting, deferring the appointment policy vote to the next meeting.
Three routine items passed unanimously: a Common Victualer license for Empire Athletics, ratifying a payroll and benefits coordinator appointment, and declaring an old stove surplus.

why_it_matters: An override signal this early means residents should expect a tax-related vote tied to the FY27 budget once school figures are finalized.
Free cash running above the budgeted assumption could fund one-time costs like the snow and ice deficit or stabilization reserves, but the town manager is not yet building it into the capital plan.
The warrant articles and goals decided at this meeting shape what residents will see and vote on at the 2026 annual town meeting.

meetings.headline: Board reviewed a proposed storm water utility fee bylaw headed to spring Town Meeting, split public reaction
meetings.summary: The Select Board ratified two new police sergeants, approved a pavilion dedication and a teen center fundraiser, and heard a lengthy joint presentation with the Planning Board and Storm Water Task Force on a proposed storm water utility bylaw and fee for spring Town Meeting. The Town Manager reported on FY27 budget preparation, building consolidation plans, and staffing, and the Board discussed warrant articles including possibly dropping the mosquito control program and legislative earmark requests; recurring public comment came from a resident opposing the storm water utility and from a family alleging town retaliation over an HOA-payment records request.

meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a lengthy town manager report warning that FY27 budget cost drivers exceed revenue growth and an override is likely, while the town's unsubmitted FY25 Schedule A risks the state withholding local aid and free cash remains uncertified. The board also honored a school resource officer for a cryptocurrency fraud recovery, marked a police officer's retirement, approved two peddler's licenses, voted to retain labor counsel under his new firm, and began discussing FY27 legislative earmark requests and warrant articles for town meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said health insurance, retirement assessment and school transportation are major cost drivers exceeding revenue growth, and that absent service reductions an override is likely required.
The town has not submitted the Schedule A to the Division of Local Services; failure to do so by February 13th risks the state withholding local aid.
Free cash has not yet been certified, which directly affects planning for town meeting including the capital plan, reserve transfers, and the snow and ice deficit.

A preliminary capital plan was delivered but is conservative pending free cash certification; two large projects, the Flatill road bridge and the public safety roof, are consuming much of the available funding.
The town is in deficit spending for snow and ice after 18 snow events this season; this is legally permitted deficit spending.
The DPW director and stormwater task force will present a proposed budget for a new storm water utility to the finance committee and later to a joint board meeting.
The town now bears full TCP building operating costs after the school department vacated; expected energy savings from partial decommissioning have not materialized.
The town applied for a MassDOT grant to fund design of the Goodrich Street culvert over Easterbrook Brook.
The town believes moving with Attorney Terry to his new, more public-sector-focused firm will be a cost savings over time; there are no hourly rates cited.
The board reviewed past state earmarks received by the town, mostly for schools, and discussed shifting focus toward town-side requests for the FY27 state budget.
A draft warrant article proposes a multi-year allocation for the town's 300th anniversary.
A second draft warrant article would establish a gift fund for donations and sale of anniversary merchandise.
The school committee discussed using funds originally for a new literacy coach position instead to build internal capacity by paying existing skilled staff stipends.
The school committee added a five-day preschool option alongside 2, 3, and 4-day options, with an annual tuition increase; this passed.
The school committee had discussed the school budget using certain healthcare figures, but has since learned those healthcare numbers are lower and will need to adjust the budget accordingly.

decisions.decision: Town manager to continue pursuing an official extension from DLS of the February 13th Schedule A deadline.
Town manager began meeting individually with TCP building user groups to discuss a possible wind-down of remaining building operations.
Chair will reach out to the school committee about crafting a joint warrant article on the Kids Kingdom relocation.
Deadline for other boards/committees to submit warrant articles for town meeting is set at March 16th.
Board deferred voting on four sets of 2024 minutes to a future meeting since only three members were present and one would abstain.
The February 9th tri-board meeting may need to be rescheduled, pending confirmation.

what_happened.line: The town manager and board warned the FY27 budget season will be difficult, worsened by vacancies in the finance department.
Nashoba Associated Boards of Health voted to raise its assessment on the town, citing a structural funding shortfall.
Eleven water customers missed regular quarterly bills after a staffing-transition breakdown and will get catch-up bills; a rate adjustment is expected next week.
A school committee budget workshop found paraprofessionals left out of the FY26 school budget; a superintendent's letter is expected to explain the correction.
The board voted to open the annual town meeting warrant, to close March 16, 2026.

why_it_matters: A strained finance office heading into budget season can slow the numbers residents will eventually vote on at town meeting.
A higher regional health assessment and an FY26 school budget correction both press on the same town budget that funds services and schools.
The eleven affected water customers will see a larger-than-usual bill covering roughly a year of missed usage, and other customers may see a rate change follow.
